books.section: Topic 8.2 The Cold War from 1945 to 1980
America in an Era of Turmoil (1960-1975)
Unit 8: The Postwar Period and Cold War (1945-1980)

primary_sources: John F. Kennedy, address on the Cuban Missile Crisis, October 22, 1962 (paraphrased in the question)

stimulus.source_note: Original summary passage written for this question; facts from the grounding books.
stimulus.text: In October 1962, American reconnaissance photographs showed Soviet missile sites under construction in Cuba, ninety miles from Florida. President John Kennedy announced a naval quarantine of the island and demanded the missiles be removed. For thirteen days the world waited while the two sides negotiated in secret. Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev agreed to withdraw the missiles, and the United States privately promised to remove its missiles from Turkey.

source: original; stimulus is an original summary passage written for this question
stem: The secret American promise to remove missiles from Turkey is most significant because it shows that the crisis ended through

options.text: a unilateral Soviet surrender with no American concession.
options.misconception: The Turkey promise was an American concession, so the ending was not one-sided.

options.text: a negotiated compromise in which both sides gave ground.
a vote of the United Nations Security Council.
options.misconception: The deal was struck in secret letters, not by a United Nations vote.

options.text: an American invasion of Cuba that removed Castro.
options.misconception: No invasion happened; Castro remained in power after the crisis.

rationales.A: The United States did give something up, privately promising to remove its Jupiter missiles from Turkey. A surrender with no concession would not include that promise.
rationales.B: Khrushchev withdrew the missiles from Cuba, and Kennedy privately promised to withdraw American missiles from Turkey. Background from the books: the deal was kept secret so neither leader would look weak at home.
rationales.C: The United Nations debated the crisis, but no Security Council vote settled it. The settlement came from secret letters between Kennedy and Khrushchev.
rationales.D: The United States never invaded Cuba in 1962, and Castro stayed in power. The crisis ended with the missiles withdrawn, not with an invasion.
rationales.general:
1. The passage says the missiles left Cuba, and it also says the United States privately promised to remove its missiles from Turkey.
2. Two withdrawals, one public and one secret, mean both sides moved, not just one.
3. The secrecy matters too: each leader needed the deal to look like strength at home.
Remember: When a crisis ends quietly, look for the concession that was kept out of the headlines.
